title: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES
alt_titles: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES, WITH OR WITHOUT MICROCORNEA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that multiple types of cataract (CTRCT2), with or without microcornea, are caused by heterozygous mutation in the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC) on chromosome 2q33-q35.

checks.claim: Multiple types of cataract (CTRCT2), with or without microcornea, are caused by heterozygous mutation in the CRYGC gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Further analysis of the original Coppock-like-cataract family identified a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of CRYGC.
checks.explanation: Abstract supports a CRYGC mutation causing Coppock-like cataract only; heterozygosity, multiple cataract types, and microcornea are not mentioned in the abstract.

checks.claim: The CRYGC gene is located on chromosome 2q33-q35.
checks.evidence_quote: We recently mapped the aculeiform cataract to the gamma-crystallin locus (CRYG) on chromosome 2q33-35, and mutational analysis of the CRYG-genes cluster
checks.explanation: CRYGC is part of the CRYG cluster located at 2q33-35.

paragraphs.text: CTRCT2 is an autosomal dominant congenital cataract that maps to the gamma-crystallin gene cluster on chromosome 2q33-q35. The lens opacities vary in type. Reported forms include Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus, zonular pulverulent cataract, and nuclear cataract. In some families, the cataract occurs together with microcornea, nystagmus, and amblyopia.

paragraphs.text: Scott et al. (1994) described a 7-generation family in which 48 of 138 individuals were known to have autosomal dominant congenital cataracts of the pulverulent type. Fifty-three family members were examined, and 28 of them had congenital cataracts. Of these 28 patients, 19 had unilateral cataract (8 right eyes and 11 left eyes) and 9 had bilateral cataract. In patients with unilateral cataract, the clinically unaffected eye showed no lenticular opacity on detailed slit-lamp examination. Severity ranged from a subtle unilateral zonular cataract with 20/20 visual acuity, and bilateral inner fetal nuclear pulverulent opacities with 20/16 visual acuity in both eyes, to dense unilateral and bilateral nuclear cataracts that needed early surgical removal. When historical data on unexamined members were included, there were 48 affected members: 28 unilateral, 17 bilateral, and 3 obligate carriers who were not examined. The authors stated that, to their knowledge, this was the first family described with apparently random expression of an autosomal dominant cataract gene as either unilateral or bilateral cataract.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2009) studied a 4-generation Chinese family from a relatively isolated region of northern China. Six members had congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea, with no other ocular or systemic abnormalities. The affected individuals had bilateral central nuclear opacities involving the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nucleus of the lens. They also had congenitally small eyeballs and corneas with a diameter of approximately 9 to 10 mm. All affected individuals had the same poor visual acuity of hand movements in front of the eye, and all had nystagmus and amblyopia.

paragraphs.text: Guo et al. (2012) reported a 4-generation Chinese family in which 6 members had isolated bilateral nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The nuclear opacities involved the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nuclei, and the corneal diameter was approximately 9 mm in all affected individuals. The proband was diagnosed at 8 years of age and underwent iridectomy on both eyes at that age. At age 38 he had phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation in the left eye. His best corrected visual acuity was 0.08 in the right eye and counting fingers at 30 cm in the left eye. Two other affected individuals were first diagnosed at 6 months and 1 year of age. Intraocular pressure was normal. All patients had nystagmus and amblyopia, and there was no history of related systemic abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Several families have shown autosomal dominant transmission of CTRCT2 (Lubsen et al., 1987; Scott et al., 1994; Ren et al., 2000; Gonzalez-Huerta et al., 2007). In the family reported by Zhang et al. (2009), affected individuals appeared in each of 4 generations and there was male-to-male transmission. Penetrance appeared to be virtually complete in that family.

paragraphs.text: In a family with Coppock-like cataract, Lubsen et al. (1987) found that a gamma-crystallin cluster haplotype defined by TaqI RFLPs (haplotype P) was present only in affected members, and that all affected members carried it. This established close linkage between the cataract locus and the gamma-crystallin gene cluster, with a maximum lod score of 7.58 at theta = 0.

paragraphs.text: In the family with variable zonular pulverulent cataract, Ren et al. (2000) found no abnormalities in the CRYGD gene. They identified a 5-bp duplication in exon 2 of the CRYGC gene in 1 allele of each affected family member. The duplication was absent from unaffected family members and from unaffected controls. It disrupts the reading frame and is predicted to produce an unstable gamma-C-crystallin containing 38 amino acids of the first Greek key motif followed by 52 random amino acids.

paragraphs.text: In a 3-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract, Li et al. (2012) used candidate gene sequencing to identify a heterozygous missense mutation in the CRYGC gene (G129C). In zebrafish, the mutant protein caused vacuoles and incomplete denucleation of the lens, reproducing the cataract phenotype. Molecular modeling and spectroscopic studies indicated that the mutation impaired the tertiary structure of the protein by modifying the H-bonding network in the C-terminal domain. The mutation also markedly reduced thermal stability and increased the tendency to aggregate under stress from storage at high concentration, heat, and UV irradiation.

paragraphs.text: In a 4-generation Chinese family with congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea, Guo et al. paragraphs.text: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) studied the Coppock-like cataract family. They found that the CRYGD gene cloned from the disease chromosome was functionally equivalent to its wildtype allele. The CRYGE pseudogene on the disease chromosome, however, contained a cluster of sequence changes within and around its TATA box. Together these changes increased promoter activity 10-fold, raising expression of the pseudogene to 30% of that of CRYGD. The authors proposed that reactivation of the pseudogene, with overexpression of a predicted 6-kD N-terminal gamma-crystallin fragment, could cause the cataract. Héon et al. (1999) later found that this CRYGE change was a polymorphism present in 23% of their control population. They then identified a CRYGC missense mutation in the original family. In the family with zonular pulverulent cataract, Ren et al. (2000) also concluded that activation of the CRYGE pseudogene was unlikely to cause the disease. They found base changes in the TATA box, but not in the Sp1-binding site, in unaffected controls.

paragraphs.text: In a 7-generation family with highly variable autosomal dominant zonular pulverulent cataract (Scott et al., 1994), Ren et al. (2000) identified a 5-bp duplication in exon 2 of the CRYGC gene in 1 allele of every affected family member. The duplication was absent from unaffected family members and from controls. It disrupts the reading frame and is predicted to produce an unstable gamma-C-crystallin with 38 amino acids of the first Greek key motif followed by 52 random amino acids. Guo et al. (2012) listed this mutation as c.123-128insGCGGC.

paragraphs.text: In a 4-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea, Zhang et al.
